stem: Park sues Hale for breach of a loan agreement and files the complaint on March 2, 2026. On April 6, to save money, Park personally hands Hale a copy of the summons and complaint at Hale's home. The summons bears the clerk's signature but no court seal. Assume the forum state's service rules allow nothing beyond Rule 4(e)(2). Hale does not answer. On June 8, Hale serves a motion under Rule 12(b)(5) arguing that service was insufficient; the motion raises no other defense. Park's response gives no explanation for serving the papers himself. On June 15, before the court rules, Hale serves a second motion, this time under Rule 12(b)(4), arguing that the summons is defective because it lacks the court's seal. On June 22, Park serves an amended complaint that adds a claim against Hale for breach of a different promise in the same loan agreement. Hale objects that Park may not amend while two motions are pending.
ask: Analyze Hale's two motions and Park's amended complaint, and explain how the court should rule on each.

rubric.point: Only a non-party adult may serve process. Park is a party and handed over the papers himself, so the April 6 delivery was not valid service.
rubric.quote: Any person who is at least 18 years old and not a party may serve a summons and complaint.

rubric.point: Hale moved before answering, so the June 8 Rule 12(b)(5) motion is a proper way to raise insufficient service.
rubric.quote: A motion asserting any of these defenses must be made before pleading if a responsive pleading is allowed.

rubric.point: More than 90 days passed after the March 2 filing with no valid service, so on Hale's motion the court must dismiss without prejudice or order service within a specified time.
rubric.quote: If a defendant is not served within 90 days after the complaint is filed, the court-on motion or on its own after notice to the plaintiff-must dismiss the action without prejudice against that defendant or order that service be made within a specified time.

rubric.point: Good cause is what compels an extension. Park offers no explanation, so no showing compels one and the court chooses between dismissal without prejudice and an order setting a time for service.
rubric.quote: But if the plaintiff shows good cause for the failure, the court must extend the time for service for an appropriate period.

rubric.point: A summons must bear the court's seal, so the missing seal is a genuine defect in process under Rule 12(b)(4).
rubric.quote: bear the court's seal

rubric.point: The seal defect was available when Hale made the first motion but was omitted from it, so the June 15 second Rule 12 motion is barred.
rubric.quote: a party that makes a motion under this rule must not make another motion under this rule raising a defense or objection that was available to the party but omitted from its earlier motion.

rubric.point: Omitting a Rule 12(b)(2)-(5) defense from a motion in the Rule 12(g)(2) circumstances waives it, so Hale waived insufficient process.
rubric.quote: omitting it from a motion in the circumstances described in Rule 12(g)(2)

rubric.point: A complaint requires a responsive pleading, so Park may amend once as of course within 21 days after service of the Rule 12(b) motion; June 22 is within 21 days of June 8.
rubric.quote: 21 days after service of a responsive pleading or 21 days after service of a motion under Rule 12(b), (e), or (f), whichever is earlier.

rubric.point: The new claim against the same opposing party may be joined as another claim.
rubric.quote: may join, as independent or alternative claims, as many claims as it has against an opposing party

model:
Service. Rule 4(c)(2) lets only a non-party who is at least 18 serve process. Park is a party, so his April 6 hand delivery was not valid service and Hale's insufficient-service defense is correct on the merits. Hale raised it by motion before answering, as Rule 12(b) requires, so it is preserved.

Remedy. Rule 4(m) allows 90 days after filing to serve. That period ended about June 1 (day 90, May 31, was a Sunday), with no valid service. On Hale's motion the court must either dismiss without prejudice or order service within a specified time. Good cause would require an extension, but Park offers no explanation, so nothing compels one; the court may choose either remedy, including a short deadline for proper re-service.

Second motion. Rule 4(a)(1)(G) requires the summons to bear the court's seal, so the omission is a Rule 12(b)(4) defect. But it was available to Hale on June 8. Rule 12(g)(2) forbids a party that makes a Rule 12 motion from making another raising a defense that was available but omitted, and Rule 12(h)(1)(A) says omitting a Rule 12(b)(2)-(5) defense in those circumstances waives it. Hale therefore waived insufficient process, and the court should deny the second motion. The first motion, which raised insufficient service, is unaffected.

Amendment. Park's complaint requires a responsive pleading, so Rule 15(a)(1)(B) lets him amend once as a matter of course within 21 days after service of a Rule 12(b) motion. June 22 falls inside the 21 days that began on June 8, so he needed no leave, and the rule expressly contemplates amendment after such a motion. The added claim against the same opposing party is a permitted joinder under Rule 18(a).

Conclusion. Act on the first motion under Rule 4(m), deny the second as barred and waived, and treat the amended complaint as properly served.

stem: Ortiz Plumbing sues Vance Pike and Pike Supply Co. on January 5, 2026. Ortiz and both defendants are located in the United States. On January 12, Ortiz sends each defendant a request to waive service that complies with Rule 4(d)(1) and allows 30 days to respond. Vance signs and returns the waiver on February 2 and serves an answer on March 12. Pike Supply ignores the request and gives no reason. On February 24, an adult friend of Ortiz hands the summons and complaint to Pike Supply's president. On March 10, Pike Supply serves a Rule 12(e) motion for a more definite statement; on March 24 the court denies it and sets no different time. Pike Supply's lawyer, who had calendared the answer from February 24 and overlooked the March 24 order, serves an answer on April 9. He moves for an order accepting it as timely, calling the error an honest oversight. Ortiz opposes that motion and moves for the cost of the second service.
ask: Analyze when each defendant's answer was due, whether each was timely, and how the court should rule on the two motions.

rubric.point: Vance timely returned a waiver before being served, so his answer was not due until 60 days after the January 12 request, March 13; his March 12 answer was timely.
rubric.quote: A defendant who, before being served with process, timely returns a waiver need not serve an answer to the complaint until 60 days after the request was sent

rubric.point: Pike Supply did not waive, so its baseline answer time runs 21 days from service on February 24, which would be March 17.
rubric.quote: within 21 days after being served with the summons and complaint

rubric.point: Delivery to Pike Supply's president, an officer, is proper service on a corporation, so the 21-day clock started February 24.
rubric.quote: delivering a copy of the summons and of the complaint to an officer, a managing or general agent, or any other agent authorized by appointment or by law to receive service of process

rubric.point: The March 10 motion came before any responsive pleading, so it was timely made.
rubric.quote: The motion must be made before filing a responsive pleading

rubric.point: After the court denied the motion on March 24, the answer was due 14 days after notice of that action, April 7, so the April 9 answer was two days late.
rubric.quote: if the court denies the motion or postpones its disposition until trial, the responsive pleading must be served within 14 days after notice of the court's action

rubric.point: Pike Supply failed without good cause to sign and return the requested waiver, so the court must impose the later service expenses and the reasonable expenses, including fees, of a motion required to collect them.
rubric.quote: If a defendant located within the United States fails, without good cause, to sign and return a waiver requested by a plaintiff located within the United States, the court must impose on the defendant:

rubric.point: The court has authority to extend a time for good cause.
rubric.quote: the court may, for good cause, extend the time

rubric.point: After the time has expired, an extension requires a motion and a failure to act because of excusable neglect; whether this oversight qualifies is for the court.
rubric.quote: on motion made after the time has expired if the party failed to act because of excusable neglect

model:
Vance. He returned the waiver on February 2, before any service and within the time allowed. Rule 4(d)(3) and Rule 12(a)(1)(A)(ii) give him 60 days after the January 12 request, so his answer was due March 13. His March 12 answer was timely.

Pike Supply's deadline. The president is an officer, so delivery to him was proper service under Rule 4(h)(1)(B) (the server was a non-party adult, as Rule 4(c)(2) requires). The baseline under Rule 12(a)(1)(A)(i) is 21 days from February 24, or March 17. But Pike Supply made its Rule 12(e) motion on March 10, before answering, as Rule 12(e) requires. When the court denies such a motion, Rule 12(a)(4)(A) requires the responsive pleading within 14 days after notice of the court's action unless the court sets another time. Notice came March 24, so the answer was due April 7. The April 9 answer was two days late.

Late answer. Rule 6(b)(1)(B) allows the court, for good cause, to extend a time on motion made after it expires if the party failed to act because of excusable neglect. Misreading the calendar is the kind of showing the court weighs, but the rule leaves the question to its judgment, so the court may grant the motion; it is not required to.

Service costs. Ortiz and the defendants are all in the United States, Ortiz requested a waiver, and Pike Supply ignored it without good cause. Under Rule 4(d)(2) the court must impose the expenses of the later service and the reasonable expenses, including attorney's fees, of the motion needed to collect them. Ortiz's motion should be granted.

Conclusion. Vance timely; Pike Supply late by two days, with relief discretionary; costs mandatory.

stem: Danner sues Brisk Couriers Inc. for $50,000 for a lost shipment of dental equipment that Brisk agreed to deliver to her clinic. Brisk serves its answer on June 1, 2026. It then determines that its subcontractor, Nolan Freight, lost the shipment under a written contract making Nolan responsible to Brisk for any loss in transit. On June 22, Brisk serves a third-party summons and complaint on Nolan that (1) seeks reimbursement of whatever Brisk owes Danner and (2) adds a separate claim for $8,000 that Nolan owes Brisk on an unrelated invoice. Brisk has not asked the court's permission. Danner, worried about delay, moves to sever the third-party claims and also serves a claim of her own directly against Nolan for the same loss. Nolan, for its part, wants to bring in Ames Storage, the warehouse that actually mishandled the shipment and that Nolan hired to hold it overnight under a contract promising to cover any loss in its care. The court has not yet ruled on anything.
ask: Discuss Brisk's right to implead Nolan, Danner's motion, Danner's own claim, and Nolan's plan, and say how the court should rule.

rubric.point: Brisk is a defending party and Nolan is a nonparty who may be liable to it for the lost-shipment claim, so impleader is available.
rubric.quote: A defending party may, as third-party plaintiff, serve a summons and complaint on a nonparty who is or may be liable to it for all or part of the claim against it.

rubric.point: June 22 is 21 days after the June 1 answer, more than 14, so Brisk must obtain leave by motion; it did not.
rubric.quote: But the third-party plaintiff must, by motion, obtain the court's leave if it files the third-party complaint more than 14 days after serving its original answer.

rubric.point: The unrelated $8,000 invoice claim may be joined, because a party asserting a third-party claim may join as many claims as it has against the opposing party.
rubric.quote: A party asserting a claim, counterclaim, crossclaim, or third-party claim may join, as independent or alternative claims, as many claims as it has against an opposing party.

rubric.point: Any party may move to sever or try separately, so Danner's concern about delay is a proper subject of a motion.
rubric.quote: Any party may move to strike the third-party claim, to sever it, or to try it separately.

rubric.point: Danner's claim against Nolan arises out of the same shipment loss that is the subject of her claim against Brisk, so she may assert it.
rubric.quote: The plaintiff may assert against the third-party defendant any claim arising out of the transaction or occurrence that is the subject matter of the plaintiff's claim against the third-party plaintiff.

rubric.point: As a third-party defendant, Nolan may proceed against Ames, a nonparty who may be liable to Nolan for the claim.
rubric.quote: A third-party defendant may proceed under this rule against a nonparty who is or may be liable to the third-party defendant for all or part of any claim against it.

model:
Right to implead. Rule 14(a)(1) lets a defending party serve a summons and complaint on a nonparty who is or may be liable to it for all or part of the claim against it. Brisk is the defending party, and Nolan's contract makes it responsible to Brisk for the lost shipment, so Nolan is a proper third-party defendant.

Leave. Brisk served its third-party complaint 21 days after its original answer. Rule 14(a)(1) requires the third-party plaintiff to obtain the court's leave, by motion, when it files more than 14 days after serving the answer. Brisk did not, so its service is defective as it stands. Brisk should move for leave now; the rule states no standard, so the court may grant or deny it.

Joinder of the invoice claim. Rule 18(a) lets a party asserting a third-party claim join as many claims as it has against the opposing party, so the unrelated $8,000 claim may ride along with the reimbursement claim.

Danner's motion. Rule 14(a)(4) allows any party to move to strike the third-party claim, sever it, or try it separately. Danner's concern about delay may justify severing or separate trial of the third-party claims; the rule leaves that choice to the court.

Danner's claim. Rule 14(a)(3) permits the plaintiff to assert against the third-party defendant any claim arising out of the transaction or occurrence that is the subject of her claim against the third-party plaintiff. The same lost shipment underlies both, so she may sue Nolan directly.

Nolan's plan. Rule 14(a)(5) lets a third-party defendant proceed under the rule against a nonparty who is or may be liable to it for all or part of the claim against it. Ames fits that description, so Nolan may implead it.

Conclusion. Impleader is proper in substance but requires leave; the court may grant it and may also sever.

stem: Lin sues Orchard Builders and Westin Supply in one complaint for water damage to her house, alleging that Orchard negligently installed the roof and Westin sold the defective shingles. Orchard serves an answer on September 14, 2026 that includes a crossclaim against Westin asserting that, if Orchard is liable to Lin, Westin must reimburse Orchard for that liability. On October 5, Westin serves an answer to the crossclaim and also states a claim against Orchard for $12,000 in unpaid invoices for the same shingles, and a similar claim against Pell, Orchard's owner, who personally guaranteed those invoices. Pell, a nonparty until now, moves to dismiss for misjoinder, arguing that his guaranty is a separate contract and that he has no connection to Lin's lawsuit. Orchard separately objects that Lin should not have been allowed to sue both defendants together, because she charges negligence against one and a product defect against the other.
ask: Analyze whether Lin could join both defendants, whether Orchard's crossclaim is proper, whether Westin's answer was timely and its claims proper, and how the court should rule on Pell's motion.

rubric.point: Lin asserts a right to relief against both defendants arising out of the same water damage, so they may be joined as defendants.
rubric.quote: any right to relief is asserted against them jointly, severally, or in the alternative with respect to or arising out of the same transaction, occurrence, or series of transactions or occurrences

rubric.point: Orchard's objection fails because a defendant need not be interested in defending against all the relief demanded; different theories against each do not defeat joinder.
rubric.quote: Neither a plaintiff nor a defendant need be interested in obtaining or defending against all the relief demanded.

rubric.point: Orchard's claim against Westin, a coparty, arises out of the roof and shingles that are the subject of Lin's original action, so it is a proper crossclaim.
rubric.quote: A pleading may state as a crossclaim any claim by one party against a coparty if the claim arises out of the transaction or occurrence that is the subject matter of the original action

rubric.point: A crossclaim may assert that the coparty is or may be liable to the crossclaimant for all or part of the claim against the crossclaimant, which is Orchard's reimbursement theory.
rubric.quote: The crossclaim may include a claim that the coparty is or may be liable to the crossclaimant for all or part of a claim asserted in the action against the crossclaimant.

rubric.point: Westin's answer was due 21 days after service of the crossclaim pleading, September 14 plus 21 days is October 5, so it was timely.
rubric.quote: A party must serve an answer to a counterclaim or crossclaim within 21 days after being served with the pleading that states the counterclaim or crossclaim.

rubric.point: Westin's invoice claim arises out of the same shingle sale that is the subject of Orchard's crossclaim, so Westin must state it as a counterclaim, and it did.
rubric.quote: A pleading must state as a counterclaim any claim that-at the time of its service-the pleader has against an opposing party if the claim:

rubric.point: Adding Pell as a party to a counterclaim is governed by the ordinary joinder rules, Rules 19 and 20.
rubric.quote: Rules 19 and 20 govern the addition of a person as a party to a counterclaim or crossclaim.

rubric.point: Misjoinder is not a ground for dismissing an action, and the court may drop a party or sever a claim on just terms, so Pell's motion to dismiss fails even if he is misjoined.
rubric.quote: Misjoinder of parties is not a ground for dismissing an action. On motion or on its own, the court may at any time, on just terms, add or drop a party. The court may also sever any claim against a party.

model:
Lin's joinder of defendants. Rule 20(a)(2) permits joining defendants if a right to relief is asserted against them jointly, severally or in the alternative arising out of the same occurrence, and a common question will arise. Lin claims one water-damage event from the same roof, so the requirement is met. Rule 20(a)(3) answers Orchard's objection: a defendant need not be interested in defending against all the relief demanded, so different theories against each do not defeat joinder.

Orchard's crossclaim. Rule 13(g) allows a pleading to state as a crossclaim any claim by one party against a coparty arising out of the transaction that is the subject of the original action, and it may include a claim that the coparty is or may be liable to the crossclaimant for all or part of the claim against the crossclaimant. Orchard and Westin are coparties, and the claim concerns the same roof and shingles, so the crossclaim is proper.

Westin's response. Rule 12(a)(1)(B) requires an answer to a crossclaim within 21 days after service of the pleading stating it. Twenty-one days after September 14 is October 5, so Westin was timely. Its invoice claim against Orchard arises from the same shingle sale that is the subject of Orchard's crossclaim, so Rule 13(a)(1) makes it a counterclaim that Westin must state; stating it now satisfies the rule, and even if it were not compulsory Rule 13(b) would allow it.

Pell. Rule 13(h) says Rules 19 and 20 govern adding a person as a party to a counterclaim. Westin asserts relief severally against Orchard and Pell for the same invoices, and the common question is whether the invoices are owed. Even if Pell were misjoined, Rule 21 says misjoinder is not a ground for dismissal; the court may drop him or sever the claim on just terms. Pell's motion to dismiss should be denied.

stem: Three tenants sue Larkin Management and its heating contractor, Pierce Heating, in one complaint. Alma and Ben, who live in Building A, allege that a faulty furnace installed by Pierce and maintained by Larkin leaked carbon monoxide into both apartments in January 2026. Cole lives in Building C and alleges that in March 2026 a burst pipe, which Larkin failed to repair after repeated complaints, flooded his unit. Cole asserts no claim against Pierce, and Pierce had nothing to do with the pipe. Alma's complaint also includes a claim that Larkin wrongfully kept her $1,500 security deposit. Pierce moves to dismiss the whole action for misjoinder, arguing that Cole's claim has nothing to do with the carbon monoxide leak and that it should not have to sit through a trial about Cole's flood. Larkin separately argues that Alma cannot sue it for the deposit in the same case as her carbon monoxide claim.
ask: Analyze Pierce's motion and Larkin's objection, and explain how the court should rule.

rubric.point: Alma and Ben assert rights to relief arising out of the same January leak, so they may join as plaintiffs.
rubric.quote: they assert any right to relief jointly, severally, or in the alternative with respect to or arising out of the same transaction, occurrence, or series of transactions or occurrences

rubric.point: Alma and Ben also share common questions, such as whether the furnace was faulty.
rubric.quote: any question of law or fact common to all plaintiffs will arise in the action

rubric.point: The relief against Larkin and Pierce for the leak arises from the same occurrence, so they may be joined as defendants as to Alma and Ben.
rubric.quote: any right to relief is asserted against them jointly, severally, or in the alternative with respect to or arising out of the same transaction, occurrence, or series of transactions or occurrences

rubric.point: Cole's March flood in another building, from a different cause and against only Larkin, is not part of the same transaction or occurrence as the January leak; he is likely misjoined as a plaintiff.
rubric.quote: they assert any right to relief jointly, severally, or in the alternative with respect to or arising out of the same transaction, occurrence, or series of transactions or occurrences

rubric.point: Even so, misjoinder is not a ground for dismissing the action.
rubric.quote: Misjoinder of parties is not a ground for dismissing an action.

rubric.point: The court may drop a party or sever Cole's claim on just terms.
rubric.quote: On motion or on its own, the court may at any time, on just terms, add or drop a party. The court may also sever any claim against a party.

rubric.point: A plaintiff or defendant need not be involved in all the relief demanded, so Pierce's lack of involvement with Cole's claim does not defeat the others' joinder.
rubric.quote: Neither a plaintiff nor a defendant need be interested in obtaining or defending against all the relief demanded.

rubric.point: The court may order separate trials to protect Pierce, a party against whom Cole asserts no claim.
rubric.quote: The court may issue orders-including an order for separate trials-to protect a party against embarrassment, delay, expense, or other prejudice that arises from including a person against whom the party asserts no claim and who asserts no claim against the party.

rubric.point: Alma may add her deposit claim, because a party asserting a claim may join as many claims as it has against an opposing party.
rubric.quote: may join, as independent or alternative claims, as many claims as it has against an opposing party

model:
Alma, Ben and the furnace. Rule 20(a)(1) lets persons join as plaintiffs if they assert a right to relief arising out of the same transaction or occurrence and a common question will arise. Alma and Ben allege one January leak in one building, and whether the furnace was faulty is common to both. Rule 20(a)(2) likewise allows Larkin and Pierce to be joined as defendants because relief for that leak is sought against both.

Cole. Cole's flood happened two months later, in another building, from a burst pipe, and is asserted only against Larkin. It does not arise out of the same transaction or occurrence as the leak, and the facts do not suggest a related series, so Cole is likely misjoined under Rule 20(a)(1)(A). But Pierce asks for dismissal of the whole action, and Rule 21 says misjoinder is not a ground for dismissing an action. Rule 21 instead allows the court, on motion or on its own, to drop a party or sever any claim on just terms. The court should deny dismissal and may sever Cole's claim or drop Cole as a plaintiff.

Pierce's concern. Rule 20(a)(3) provides that a defendant need not be interested in defending against all the relief demanded, so Pierce's lack of involvement in Cole's claim does not defeat the others' joinder. If Cole remains, Rule 20(b) lets the court order separate trials to protect a party from prejudice or expense arising from a person against whom it asserts no claim and who asserts none against it. Cole asserts no claim against Pierce, so Pierce is within that protection.

Alma's deposit claim. Rule 18(a) lets a party asserting a claim join as many claims as it has against an opposing party. Alma is already suing Larkin, so she may add the deposit claim although unrelated. Larkin's objection fails.

Conclusion. Deny dismissal; sever or drop Cole's claim, or try it separately; deposit claim allowed.

stem: On March 3, 2024, a delivery truck owned by Harlan Freight Inc. strikes Reyes's car. Because the truck and the driver's uniform say "Harlan Trucking," Reyes sues Harlan Trucking LLC, an affiliate that shares an office and a registered agent with Harlan Freight, in a complaint filed February 10, 2026. A two-year limitation period for the claim expired March 3, 2026. Harlan Trucking serves an answer on March 2 saying it did not own the truck. A copy of the complaint was delivered on February 20 to the shared registered agent, who acts for both companies, and on April 6 Harlan Freight's claims manager wrote Reyes that Freight "knew the suit was meant for us" and had been waiting to see whether Reyes would fix the name. On June 8, Reyes moves for leave to amend to substitute Harlan Freight for Harlan Trucking and to add the driver, Tabor, whose name Reyes learned only recently. Tabor first learned of the suit on June 1. Freight and Tabor oppose, arguing that the limitation period expired. Assume the applicable limitations law has no relation-back rule of its own, and that Harlan Trucking does not consent to the amendment.
ask: Analyze whether the court should permit the amendment and whether it relates back as to Freight and as to Tabor.

rubric.point: The answer was served March 2, so June 8 is past the as-of-course period; Reyes needs consent or leave, which the court should freely give when justice requires.
rubric.quote: In all other cases, a party may amend its pleading only with the opposing party's written consent or the court's leave. The court should freely give leave when justice so requires.

rubric.point: The court may add or drop parties on just terms, which is what the amendment does.
rubric.quote: On motion or on its own, the court may at any time, on just terms, add or drop a party.

rubric.point: An amendment relates back to the date of the original pleading only if one of the listed conditions is met.
rubric.quote: An amendment to a pleading relates back to the date of the original pleading when:

rubric.point: The claim against Freight arises out of the same accident set out in the original complaint.

stem: Lumen Design sues Hartley Bakery for $30,000 owed on a website build, serving the complaint on July 1, 2026. Hartley serves a timely answer on July 20, 2026 that denies owing the money and pleads no counterclaim. On July 27, Hartley serves an amended answer adding two counterclaims: (1) $18,000 for defects in the same website, and (2) $9,000 that Lumen owes Hartley for catering Lumen bought last year, which has nothing to do with the website. Hartley's lawyer explains that he left the first counterclaim out of the original answer by oversight. On August 10, before answering either counterclaim, Lumen serves a Rule 12(f) motion asking the court to strike the catering counterclaim as immaterial because it is unrelated to the website dispute and Hartley should have to sue on it separately. Lumen's lawyer adds that Lumen will not answer either counterclaim until the motion is decided. Assume the court denies the motion on August 17 and sets no different time.

rubric.point: The catering claim is not compulsory, so Hartley may, but need not, state it as a counterclaim.
rubric.quote: A pleading may state as a counterclaim against an opposing party any claim that is not compulsory.

rubric.point: Hartley may join as many claims as it has against Lumen, so unrelatedness to the website claim is no bar to the catering counterclaim and gives no basis to call it immaterial.
rubric.quote: may join, as independent or alternative claims, as many claims as it has against an opposing party

rubric.point: Hartley amended its answer 7 days after serving it, within 21 days and for the first time, so it amended as of course without leave.
rubric.quote: 21 days after serving it

rubric.point: Lumen made its Rule 12(f) motion before responding to the pleading, so the motion was timely made.
rubric.quote: on motion made by a party either before responding to the pleading or, if a response is not allowed, within 21 days after being served with the pleading.

rubric.point: Rule 12(a)(1)(B) gives 21 days after service of the pleading that states the counterclaim, so absent the motion Lumen's answer would be due August 17.
rubric.quote: A party must serve an answer to a counterclaim or crossclaim within 21 days after being served with the pleading that states the counterclaim or crossclaim.

rubric.point: After the court denies the motion on August 17, the answer is due 14 days after notice, August 31.
rubric.quote: if the court denies the motion or postpones its disposition until trial, the responsive pleading must be served within 14 days after notice of the court's action

rubric.point: Even if the amended answer counts as an amended pleading whose response runs 14 days under Rule 15(a)(3) (August 10), Lumen's August 10 motion was still timely, and the August 31 deadline is the same either way.

Compulsory counterclaim. The website-defect claim arises out of the same website contract Lumen sues on, so Hartley was required to plead it. Its original answer left it out, but the amended answer supplies it.

Permissive counterclaim. The catering claim has nothing to do with the website, so it is not compulsory. Rule 13(b) says a pleading may state as a counterclaim any claim that is not compulsory, and Rule 18(a) lets a party asserting a counterclaim join as many claims as it has against an opposing party. Hartley was therefore permitted to plead it.

Leave. Hartley served the amended answer 7 days after its answer. Rule 15(a)(1)(A) allows one amendment as of course within 21 days after serving the pleading, and an answer requires no response, so only that subparagraph applies. No leave was needed.

The motion. Lumen moved before responding, which Rule 12(f)(2) permits. But Rules 13(b) and 18(a) expressly authorize a counterclaim unrelated to the main claim, so unrelatedness cannot make the catering claim immaterial. The court should deny the motion.

Timing. Rule 12(a)(1)(B) gives Lumen 21 days after service of the amended answer to answer the counterclaims: August 17. Because Lumen served a Rule 12 motion, Rule 12(a)(4)(A) applies. Denial on August 17 makes the answer due 14 days after notice, August 31, unless the court sets another time, under either computation.

stem: Mara sues Tidewater Co-op for a declaration that she owns 100 shares of Tidewater stock registered in her name on the co-op's books. Brandt, a former business partner of Mara, also claims to own those shares, says Mara holds them only for him, and has threatened to sue Tidewater if it recognizes Mara as owner. Brandt is not a party, can be served with process, and joining him would raise no jurisdictional problem. Mara's complaint does not mention Brandt. Tidewater serves an answer on May 5, 2026 that denies Mara's ownership but does not raise the absence of Brandt. On June 2, after the pleadings are closed, Tidewater moves under Rule 12(c) for judgment on the pleadings, arguing for the first time that the case cannot go forward without Brandt, and asks that the action be dismissed. Mara responds that Tidewater waived the point by not raising it in a pre-answer motion or in its answer.
ask: Analyze whether Brandt is a person who must be joined, whether Tidewater preserved the point, and how the court should rule on the motion.

rubric.point: Brandt can be served and joining him raises no jurisdictional problem, so he is the kind of person Rule 19(a)(1) can require to be joined.
rubric.quote: A person who is subject to service of process and whose joinder will not deprive the court of subject-matter jurisdiction must be joined as a party if:

rubric.point: Brandt claims an interest in the same shares, which are the subject of the action.
rubric.quote: that person claims an interest relating to the subject of the action and is so situated that disposing of the action in the person's absence may:

rubric.point: A judgment for Mara declaring her the owner could, as a practical matter, impair Brandt's ability to protect his claimed interest in the shares.
rubric.quote: as a practical matter impair or impede the person's ability to protect the interest

rubric.point: Tidewater faces a substantial risk of double or inconsistent obligations, because Brandt threatens to sue if it recognizes Mara.
rubric.quote: leave an existing party subject to a substantial risk of incurring double, multiple, or otherwise inconsistent obligations because of the interest

rubric.point: Only the Rule 12(b)(2)-(5) defenses are waived by omission from a pre-answer motion or the answer; failure to join a person required by Rule 19(b) can still be raised later, so Mara's waiver argument fails.
rubric.quote: Failure to state a claim upon which relief can be granted, to join a person required by Rule 19(b), or to state a legal defense to a claim may be raised:

rubric.point: One listed way is a Rule 12(c) motion. Tidewater answered May 5 and moved June 2, after the pleadings closed, so the motion is a proper vehicle.
rubric.quote: by a motion under Rule 12(c)

rubric.point: The remedy for nonjoinder of a person who can be joined is an order making that person a party, not dismissal.
rubric.quote: If a person has not been joined as required, the court must order that the person be made a party.

rubric.point: Rule 19(b), which weighs dismissal, applies only if a required person cannot be joined; Brandt can be joined.
rubric.quote: If a person who is required to be joined if feasible cannot be joined, the court must determine whether, in equity and good conscience, the action should proceed among the existing parties or should be dismissed.

rubric.point: Mara's complaint, which asserts a claim for relief, never names Brandt or gives reasons for not joining him, as Rule 19(c) requires of a claimant; the omission is curable and does not itself call for dismissal.
rubric.quote: the reasons for not joining that person.

model:
Required party. Rule 19(a)(1) requires joinder of a person who is subject to service and whose joinder will not defeat subject-matter jurisdiction if, under (B), the person claims an interest relating to the subject of the action and is so situated that deciding the case without him may impair his ability to protect it or leave an existing party at risk of double or inconsistent obligations. Brandt can be served and his joinder raises no jurisdictional problem. He claims the very shares in suit. A declaration for Mara could as a practical matter impair his ability to protect that claim (Rule 19(a)(1)(B)(i)), and Tidewater, if it honors Mara's ownership, faces Brandt's threatened suit and thus a substantial risk of inconsistent obligations (Rule 19(a)(1)(B)(ii)). Brandt is a required party. Rule 19(c) required Mara, as claimant, to name any such person not joined and give the reasons; her complaint did not mention Brandt, a defect to be corrected.

Preservation. Mara argues waiver, but Rule 12(h)(1) lists only the defenses in Rule 12(b)(2)-(5) as waived by omission. Rule 12(h)(2) says failure to join a person required by Rule 19(b) may be raised in any pleading allowed under Rule 7(a), by a Rule 12(c) motion, or at trial. Tidewater's answer closed the pleadings on May 5, so its June 2 Rule 12(c) motion was an authorized vehicle.

Remedy. Tidewater asks for dismissal, but Rule 19(a)(2) says that if a person has not been joined as required, the court must order that the person be made a party. Rule 19(b), which asks whether an action should proceed or be dismissed, applies only when a required person cannot be joined, and Brandt can be.

Conclusion. Deny dismissal; order Brandt joined under Rule 19(a)(2).

stem: Dell sues Mercer Realty on September 8, 2026 for specific performance of a contract to sell Lot 12 to Dell. Mercer answers and, on October 1, tells the court it will not oppose Dell and is willing to close. On October 5, Kessler, who holds a recorded option to buy Lot 12 that a sale to Dell would defeat, mails a letter to the clerk and the parties asking to intervene "as of right" and demanding a hearing on October 12. The letter explains Kessler's option but attaches no pleading. Kessler has no lawyer and did not sign the letter. Dell opposes, arguing that the papers are defective, that Kessler's interest is already represented because Mercer owns the lot, and that intervention should be denied outright because Kessler could just sue separately. No federal statute gives Kessler a right to intervene. The case is at its earliest stage: no discovery has begun and the court has not ruled on anything.
ask: Analyze Kessler's right to intervene, the defects in his papers, and how the court should rule.

rubric.point: Kessler claims an interest in the property, an option on Lot 12, and a sale to Dell would as a practical matter impair his ability to protect it.
rubric.quote: claims an interest relating to the property or transaction that is the subject of the action, and is so situated that disposing of the action may as a practical matter impair or impede the movant's ability to protect its interest

rubric.point: Mercer has said it will not oppose Dell, so the existing parties do not adequately represent Kessler's interest.
rubric.quote: unless existing parties adequately represent that interest

rubric.point: Intervention of right requires a timely motion; Kessler moved about four weeks after suit began and before any ruling, so nothing in the facts shows untimeliness.
rubric.quote: On timely motion, the court must permit anyone to intervene who:

rubric.point: The motion must be accompanied by a pleading stating the claim or defense; Kessler attached none, a defect he should cure.
rubric.quote: The motion must state the grounds for intervention and be accompanied by a pleading that sets out the claim or defense for which intervention is sought.

rubric.point: An unrepresented party must personally sign a written motion, and Kessler did not.
rubric.quote: must be signed by at least one attorney of record in the attorney's name-or by a party personally if the party is unrepresented.

rubric.point: Because the signature omission is curable, the court must strike the unsigned paper only if the omission is not promptly corrected after being called to Kessler's attention; it should allow him to cure rather than deny outright.
rubric.quote: The court must strike an unsigned paper unless the omission is promptly corrected after being called to the attorney's or party's attention.

rubric.point: A written motion and notice of hearing must be served at least 14 days before the hearing; October 12 is seven days after October 5, and no exception is shown.
rubric.quote: A written motion and notice of the hearing must be served at least 14 days before the time specified for the hearing, with the following exceptions:

rubric.point: Alternatively, permissive intervention is available to one with a claim sharing a common question of law or fact with the main action.
rubric.quote: has a claim or defense that shares with the main action a common question of law or fact

rubric.point: Permissive intervention is discretionary, and the court must weigh undue delay or prejudice to the original parties.
rubric.quote: In exercising its discretion, the court must consider whether the intervention will unduly delay or prejudice the adjudication of the original parties' rights.

model:
Right to intervene. Rule 24(a) requires the court, on timely motion, to permit anyone to intervene who under Rule 24(a)(2) claims an interest relating to the property that is the subject of the action, is so situated that disposing of the action may as a practical matter impair the ability to protect it, and is not adequately represented by existing parties. Kessler holds a recorded option on Lot 12; an order forcing the sale to Dell would defeat it. Mercer has said it will not oppose Dell, so no existing party represents his interest. The motion came about four weeks into the case, before any ruling, so the facts do not suggest it was untimely. Dell's point that Kessler could sue separately is not a limit in Rule 24(a)(2).

Defects. Rule 24(c) requires the motion to state the grounds and be accompanied by a pleading setting out the claim or defense, and Kessler attached none. Rule 11(a) requires a written motion to be signed by an unrepresented party personally, and the court must strike an unsigned paper unless the omission is promptly corrected after being called to his attention. His demand for an October 12 hearing also fails Rule 6(c)(1), which requires service of a written motion and notice of hearing at least 14 days before the hearing absent a listed exception, and seven days is not enough. These are curable: he may file a signed motion with a pleading and a proper hearing date.

Alternative. If the court found a defect in the right claim, Rule 24(b)(1)(B) lets it permit anyone to intervene who has a claim sharing a common question of law or fact with the main action; Kessler's claim to Lot 12 does. That is discretionary, and Rule 24(b)(3) requires the court to consider undue delay or prejudice to the original parties.

Conclusion. The court should not deny the motion outright for these defects. It should allow Kessler a short time to cure them by signing the motion, attaching a pleading and setting a proper hearing date, and then permit intervention as of right.

stem: Evans sues Metro Gym on behalf of herself and about 60 other members of Metro's Maple Street location who were each charged the same undisclosed $15 annual "maintenance fee." Metro serves its answer on March 2, 2026. On May 4, 2026, the court enters an order denying class certification, finding that 60 members at one location can practicably be joined. Evans wants to keep the other members' claims in this lawsuit and is considering several steps: asking the court of appeals to review the denial; asking the district judge to reconsider; amending the complaint to name 12 of the other members as additional plaintiffs; and having another member, Okafor, who is not named, serve a motion to intervene with a short written claim that he was charged the same fee at the same location. He would file within weeks of the May 4 order; discovery has not begun and no trial date is set. Metro answers that none of these steps is available, because the denial of certification ended any chance for the other members in this case.
ask: Advise Evans on each route for keeping the other members' claims in the case, and explain how the court should respond to Metro's position.

rubric.point: A court of appeals may permit an appeal from an order denying certification, on a petition filed with the circuit clerk within 14 days after entry; May 4 plus 14 days is May 18.
rubric.quote: A party must file a petition for permission to appeal with the circuit clerk within 14 days after the order is entered

rubric.point: An appeal does not by itself stay the district court proceedings.
rubric.quote: An appeal does not stay proceedings in the district court unless the district judge or the court of appeals so orders.

rubric.point: An order denying certification may be altered or amended before final judgment, so the district judge may reconsider.
rubric.quote: An order that grants or denies class certification may be altered or amended before final judgment.

rubric.point: The court's finding that joinder of the 60 members is practicable supports joining 12 of them as plaintiffs, and their claims arise from the same fee practice at the same location.
rubric.quote: they assert any right to relief jointly, severally, or in the alternative with respect to or arising out of the same transaction, occurrence, or series of transactions or occurrences

rubric.point: Whether the fee was disclosed is a common question for all plaintiffs.
rubric.quote: any question of law or fact common to all plaintiffs will arise in the action

rubric.point: The answer was served March 2, past the 21-day as-of-course period, so Evans needs Metro's written consent or leave to amend, and leave should be freely given when justice requires.
rubric.quote: In all other cases, a party may amend its pleading only with the opposing party's written consent or the court's leave. The court should freely give leave when justice so requires.

rubric.point: Permissive intervention requires a timely motion; Okafor would move within weeks of the order, before discovery or any trial date, so the motion appears timely.
rubric.quote: On timely motion, the court may permit anyone to intervene who:

rubric.point: Okafor has a claim sharing a common question of fact with the main action, so the court may permit him to intervene.
rubric.quote: has a claim or defense that shares with the main action a common question of law or fact

rubric.point: A motion to intervene must be accompanied by a pleading that sets out the claim; Okafor's short written claim may not qualify as a pleading, but the defect is curable by filing one.
rubric.quote: The motion must state the grounds for intervention and be accompanied by a pleading that sets out the claim or defense for which intervention is sought.

model:
Metro is wrong that denial ended everything. The ruling denied class treatment, not the members' claims, and the rules offer several routes.

Review and reconsideration. Rule 23(f) lets a court of appeals permit an appeal from an order denying certification if a party files a petition with the circuit clerk within 14 days after entry. Fourteen days from May 4 is May 18, so Evans must file by then; the court of appeals decides whether to allow it, and the appeal does not stay the district court unless an order says so. Separately, Rule 23(c)(1)(C) provides that an order denying certification may be altered or amended before final judgment, so Evans may ask the district judge to reconsider.

Joinder. The court found that joinder of 60 members is practicable, which supports adding members as ordinary plaintiffs. Under Rule 20(a)(1), persons may join as plaintiffs if they assert rights to relief arising out of the same transaction, occurrence or series, and a common question will arise. The same fee practice at the same location and the disclosure question satisfy both parts, so the court may permit the 12 members to join. Metro answered on March 2, more than 21 days ago, so Rule 15(a)(2) requires Metro's written consent or the court's leave; the court should freely give leave when justice requires.

Intervention. On timely motion, Rule 24(b)(1)(B) lets the court permit anyone to intervene who has a claim sharing a common question of law or fact with the main action. Okafor's claim does, and a motion made within weeks of the order, before discovery, appears timely. The court may deny it for undue delay or prejudice (Rule 24(b)(3)). Rule 24(c) requires a pleading setting out his claim; a short written claim may not qualify, but he can cure by filing one.

Conclusion. Evans should file the Rule 23(f) petition by May 18 and, in parallel, seek reconsideration and leave to add plaintiffs; Okafor may move to intervene.

stem: Perla sues Cross-Country Movers for damage to her antique piano during a move. Cross-Country serves its answer on October 5, 2026 and on October 15 serves a summons and third-party complaint on Axle Crating, alleging that Axle's defective crate caused the damage. The process server hands the papers to Axle's receptionist, who is not an officer or managing agent and is not authorized to receive service for Axle; assume state law adds nothing to Rule 4(h)(1)(B). Axle serves an answer on November 2 that denies liability, says nothing about service, asserts that Perla's claim is barred by a written release Perla signed in favor of Cross-Country, and asserts that Cross-Country owes Axle $4,000 for crates supplied on this same move. On November 16, Axle serves an amended answer adding an insufficient-service-of-process defense. Cross-Country objects that Axle waived that defense. Meanwhile, Perla serves a claim directly against Axle for the damage to the piano.
ask: Analyze Axle's obligations and options, whether it preserved the service defense, and Perla's claim against Axle.

rubric.point: Cross-Country served the third-party complaint 10 days after its answer, within 14 days, so it needed no leave.
rubric.quote: But the third-party plaintiff must, by motion, obtain the court's leave if it files the third-party complaint more than 14 days after serving its original answer.

rubric.point: Delivery to a receptionist who is not an officer, managing or general agent, or authorized agent is not proper service on a corporation.
rubric.quote: delivering a copy of the summons and of the complaint to an officer, a managing or general agent, or any other agent authorized by appointment or by law to receive service of process

rubric.point: As third-party defendant, Axle must assert any Rule 12 defense against Cross-Country's claim.
rubric.quote: must assert any defense against the third-party plaintiff's claim under Rule 12

rubric.point: Axle's first answer omitted the Rule 12(b)(5) defense; waiver follows unless the defense was made by motion or included in a responsive pleading or an as-of-course amendment.
rubric.quote: failing to either: (i) make it by motion under this rule; or (ii) include it in a responsive pleading or in an amendment allowed by Rule 15(a)(1) as a matter of course.

rubric.point: Axle's answer states a counterclaim, so Cross-Country must answer it, but Axle could still amend once as of course within 21 days after serving the answer; November 16 is 14 days after November 2, so the amendment was timely without leave and avoided waiver.
rubric.quote: 21 days after serving it

rubric.point: Axle's $4,000 claim arises from crates supplied on the same move, so Axle must assert it against Cross-Country as a Rule 13(a) counterclaim, and it did.
rubric.quote: must assert any counterclaim against the third-party plaintiff under Rule 13(a)

rubric.point: Axle may assert against Perla any defense Cross-Country has to her claim, such as the release Perla signed.
rubric.quote: may assert against the plaintiff any defense that the third-party plaintiff has to the plaintiff's claim

rubric.point: Perla may assert against Axle a claim arising out of the same occurrence; Axle must then assert its Rule 12 defenses and Rule 13(a) counterclaims against her.
rubric.quote: The plaintiff may assert against the third-party defendant any claim arising out of the transaction or occurrence that is the subject matter of the plaintiff's claim against the third-party plaintiff. The third-party defendant must then assert any defense under Rule 12 and any counterclaim under Rule 13(a)

model:
Impleader. Cross-Country served its third-party complaint 10 days after its answer. Rule 14(a)(1) requires leave only when the filing comes more than 14 days after the original answer, so none was needed.

Service. Rule 4(h)(1)(B) requires delivery to an officer, managing or general agent, or an agent authorized to receive process. A receptionist who is none of these is not one, and we are told state law adds nothing, so service on Axle was insufficient.

Waiver. Rule 14(a)(2)(A) requires Axle to assert its Rule 12 defenses against Cross-Country's claim, and Rule 12(h)(1)(B) waives a Rule 12(b)(2)-(5) defense unless the party makes it by motion or includes it in a responsive pleading or in an amendment allowed by Rule 15(a)(1) as a matter of course. Axle's November 2 answer omitted it. Axle's answer states a counterclaim, so Cross-Country must answer it (Rule 12(a)(1)(B)), but Rule 15(a)(1)(A) still permitted one amendment as of course within 21 days after serving the answer; Rule 15(a)(1)(B) can only extend that time. November 16 is 14 days later, so Axle's amendment was timely and, by including the defense, avoided waiver. Cross-Country's objection should fail.

Other duties and options. Rule 14(a)(2)(B) requires Axle to assert against Cross-Country any Rule 13(a) counterclaim; its $4,000 claim for crates on the same move arises out of that transaction and was pleaded. Rule 14(a)(2)(C) allows Axle to assert against Perla any defense Cross-Country has, so Axle may rely on Perla's release.

Perla's claim. Rule 14(a)(3) allows the plaintiff to assert against the third-party defendant any claim arising out of the transaction or occurrence of her claim against the third-party plaintiff. Damage to the piano during the move qualifies. Axle must then assert any Rule 12 defense and Rule 13(a) counterclaim against Perla.

Conclusion. Service defense preserved; Perla may sue Axle.

stem: Sutter sues Delta Components for breach of contract. On March 16, 2026, a process server leaves the summons and complaint with Delta's receptionist, who is not an officer or an agent authorized to receive service. On April 6, Delta serves a motion under Rule 12(b)(6) and raises no other defense. The court denies the motion on May 4 and sets no different time. On May 11, Delta serves an answer that asserts (1) insufficient service of process, because the papers were left with the receptionist; (2) failure to state a claim; and (3) failure to join Beckett, who co-signed the contract and is a person Rule 19 requires to be joined; Beckett can be served and joining him would not defeat jurisdiction. Sutter replies that Delta waived defenses (1) and (3) by omitting them from its earlier motion and that the answer is late. On May 26, Delta moves for judgment on the pleadings under Rule 12(c) on defenses (2) and (3) and attaches a sworn statement from its treasurer that the contract price was paid. Sutter opposes.
ask: Analyze Sutter's waiver and timeliness arguments and explain how the court should treat Delta's May 26 motion.

rubric.point: Delta's April 6 motion came before any pleading, as Rule 12(b) requires. After the court denied it on May 4, the responsive pleading was due 14 days after notice, May 18, so the May 11 answer was timely.
rubric.quote: if the court denies the motion or postpones its disposition until trial, the responsive pleading must be served within 14 days after notice of the court's action

rubric.point: A party that makes a Rule 12 motion may not make another raising a defense available but omitted, except as Rule 12(h)(2) or (3) provides.
rubric.quote: Except as provided in Rule 12(h)(2) or (3), a party that makes a motion under this rule must not make another motion under this rule raising a defense or objection that was available to the party but omitted from its earlier motion.

rubric.point: Delta omitted insufficient service, a Rule 12(b)(5) defense, from its first motion, so it waived that defense.
rubric.quote: omitting it from a motion in the circumstances described in Rule 12(g)(2)

rubric.point: Failure to state a claim and failure to join a person required by Rule 19(b) are not waived by omission from the motion; they may be raised in any pleading allowed under Rule 7(a), and Delta's answer is one.
rubric.quote: in any pleading allowed or ordered under Rule 7(a)

rubric.point: The pleadings closed with Delta's answer, so a Rule 12(c) motion on May 26 is a proper vehicle.
rubric.quote: After the pleadings are closed-but early enough not to delay trial-a party may move for judgment on the pleadings.

rubric.point: The treasurer's sworn statement is a matter outside the pleadings; if the court does not exclude it, the motion becomes one for summary judgment and all parties must get a reasonable opportunity to respond.
rubric.quote: If, on a motion under Rule 12(b)(6) or 12(c), matters outside the pleadings are presented to and not excluded by the court, the motion must be treated as one for summary judgment under Rule 56. All parties must be given a reasonable opportunity to present all the material that is pertinent to the motion.

rubric.point: If Beckett can be joined, the remedy on defense (3) is an order making him a party, not judgment for Delta or dismissal.
rubric.quote: If a person has not been joined as required, the court must order that the person be made a party.

model:
Timeliness. Delta's April 6 motion preceded any pleading, as Rule 12(b) requires. When the court denied it on May 4 without setting another time, Rule 12(a)(4)(A) gave Delta 14 days after notice, until May 18, to serve its answer. The May 11 answer was timely.

Insufficient service. This is a Rule 12(b)(5) defense. It was available to Delta on April 6, because the papers had been left with the receptionist weeks earlier, but Delta left it out. Rule 12(g)(2) bars a later Rule 12 motion on an omitted, available defense, and Rule 12(h)(1)(A) provides that omitting a Rule 12(b)(2)-(5) defense from a motion in those circumstances waives it. Delta waived defense (1), and restating it in the answer does not revive it.

Failure to state a claim and nonjoinder. Rule 12(g)(2) excepts what Rule 12(h)(2) permits, and Rule 12(h)(2) says failure to state a claim and failure to join a person required by Rule 19(b) may be raised in any pleading allowed under Rule 7(a), by a Rule 12(c) motion, or at trial. Rule 12(h)(1) does not waive them by omission. Delta preserved both in its answer, and Sutter's waiver argument fails as to them.

The May 26 motion. Delta's answer closed the pleadings, so Rule 12(c) is available. On defense (3), Beckett can be joined, so under Rule 19(a)(2) the court must order him made a party; judgment for Delta or dismissal is not the remedy. The treasurer's sworn statement is outside the pleadings, and payment is an affirmative defense that Rule 8(c)(1) requires to be stated in the answer, which Delta's was not. Under Rule 12(d), if the court does not exclude the statement, the motion must be treated as one for summary judgment under Rule 56, with all parties given a reasonable opportunity to respond. The court may exclude it, and Delta may seek to amend to plead payment.

Conclusion. Answer timely; defense (1) waived; defenses (2) and (3) preserved; defense (3) yields joinder, not dismissal.

stem: Okafor sues Brightwater Lumber Inc. and its yard manager, Pruitt, for injuries from a falling stack of lumber at Brightwater's yard, alleging that Pruitt ordered the unsafe stacking. Both defendants are served on February 14, 2026, and both serve answers on March 9. On March 16, Pruitt moves to dismiss for misjoinder, arguing that Okafor sues him for different conduct than Brightwater. On March 23, Brightwater serves a third-party complaint, without seeking leave, on Cedar Haulers, the carrier that stacked the lumber, alleging that Cedar's negligent stacking caused the injury and that Cedar must reimburse Brightwater for any judgment Okafor wins. On March 30, Okafor serves an amended complaint adding a claim against Brightwater for lost wages from the same injury, and Brightwater objects that Okafor needed leave to amend. On April 6, Dunn, a co-worker injured by the same stack, serves a signed motion to intervene to assert his own claim against Brightwater, attaching his complaint and arguing only that his claim shares questions of fact with Okafor's; no discovery has begun and no trial date is set. Okafor and Brightwater oppose, citing delay and the prospect of a second damages trial.
ask: Analyze each of the four disputes (Pruitt's motion, the third-party complaint, Okafor's amendment, and Dunn's motion) and say how the court should rule.

rubric.point: Okafor asserts relief against Brightwater and Pruitt for the same falling stack, and whether the stack was unsafe is a question common to both, so the two may be joined as defendants even though Pruitt's alleged conduct differs.
rubric.quote: any right to relief is asserted against them jointly, severally, or in the alternative with respect to or arising out of the same transaction, occurrence, or series of transactions or occurrences

rubric.point: Even if Pruitt were misjoined, misjoinder is not a ground for dismissal.
rubric.quote: Misjoinder of parties is not a ground for dismissing an action.

rubric.point: Brightwater may implead Cedar only because Cedar is or may be liable to Brightwater for all or part of Okafor's claim; the allegation that Cedar's stacking caused the injury and that Cedar must reimburse Brightwater supplies that liability.
rubric.quote: A defending party may, as third-party plaintiff, serve a summons and complaint on a nonparty who is or may be liable to it for all or part of the claim against it.

rubric.point: March 23 is 14 days after the March 9 answer, not more than 14, so Brightwater needed no leave to implead Cedar Haulers.
rubric.quote: But the third-party plaintiff must, by motion, obtain the court's leave if it files the third-party complaint more than 14 days after serving its original answer.

rubric.point: Okafor's complaint requires a responsive pleading, so he may amend once as of course within 21 days after service of a responsive pleading; March 30 is 21 days after March 9.
rubric.quote: 21 days after service of a responsive pleading or 21 days after service of a motion under Rule 12(b), (e), or (f), whichever is earlier.

rubric.point: The added lost-wages claim against Brightwater may be joined with the existing claim.
rubric.quote: may join, as independent or alternative claims, as many claims as it has against an opposing party

rubric.point: Permissive intervention requires a timely motion; Dunn moved about seven weeks after suit, before discovery or any trial date, so the motion appears timely.
rubric.quote: On timely motion, the court may permit anyone to intervene who:

rubric.point: Dunn has a claim that shares a common question of fact with the main action, so the court may permit him to intervene.
rubric.quote: has a claim or defense that shares with the main action a common question of law or fact

rubric.point: The decision is discretionary, and the court must consider whether intervention will unduly delay or prejudice the original parties; Dunn's motion carries a pleading as Rule 24(c) requires.
rubric.quote: In exercising its discretion, the court must consider whether the intervention will unduly delay or prejudice the adjudication of the original parties' rights.

model:
Pruitt's motion. Rule 20(a)(2) allows defendants to be joined if relief is asserted against them jointly, severally or in the alternative arising out of the same occurrence and a common question will arise. Okafor asserts relief against both for the same falling stack, and whether the stack was unsafe is common to both. Different roles do not defeat joinder. Even if joinder were improper, Rule 21 states that misjoinder is not a ground for dismissing an action; the court may add or drop a party or sever a claim on just terms. The motion should be denied.

The third-party complaint. Rule 14(a)(1) allows a defending party to implead a nonparty who is or may be liable to it for all or part of the claim against it. Brightwater alleges Cedar's stacking caused the injury and that Cedar must reimburse it for any judgment, so Cedar may be liable over to Brightwater for the claim. Leave is required only if the filing comes more than 14 days after the original answer. Brightwater answered March 9, and March 23 is exactly 14 days later, so no leave was needed.

Okafor's amendment. His complaint requires a responsive pleading, so Rule 15(a)(1)(B) lets him amend once as a matter of course within 21 days after service of a responsive pleading. March 30 is 21 days after March 9, so he needed no leave. The new claim against Brightwater is a permitted joinder under Rule 18(a).

Dunn. Rule 24(b)(1) lets the court, on timely motion, permit intervention by anyone with a claim that shares a common question of law or fact with the main action. Dunn moved about seven weeks after suit, before discovery, so the motion appears timely. His claim arises from the same stack, so the common-question standard is met, and his motion carries his pleading. The decision is discretionary, and under Rule 24(b)(3) the court must consider undue delay or prejudice to the original parties. The court may grant or deny.

Conclusion. Deny Pruitt's motion; the third-party complaint and the amendment stand; Dunn's intervention is discretionary.

Misjoinder of parties is not a ground for dismissing an action.

stem: Nolan sues Brightline Telecom as representative of about 1,800 Brightline customers who were each charged the same $12 monthly "network fee" that, Nolan alleges, the customer contract never disclosed. Nolan's own claim is for the same fee. Each member's damages are small, the fee is applied by one billing system, and whether the contract disclosed it is the main contested question. Nolan moves for certification under Rule 23(b)(3). On September 1, 2026, the court certifies a class defined by the fee. The order says nothing about class counsel, and it directs notice by a single newspaper advertisement, although Brightline holds every customer's mailing and email address. Brightline wants review and files a petition for permission to appeal with the circuit clerk on September 14. Later, Nolan and Brightline agree to dismiss the case on Brightline's payment of $5,000 to Nolan alone, with nothing for the class and no notice to its members.
ask: Evaluate whether this action meets Rule 23, and analyze the defects in the certification order, Brightline's petition, and the proposed dismissal.

rubric.point: All four prerequisites are met: about 1,800 customers make joinder impracticable, whether the contract disclosed the fee is common to all, and Nolan's claim for the same fee is typical. No conflict appears at certification, so he adequately represents the class then; the later side deal for him alone is the contrary signal.
rubric.quote: One or more members of a class may sue or be sued as representative parties on behalf of all members only if:

rubric.point: For a damages class, common questions must predominate and a class action must be superior; small identical claims from one billing system fit.
rubric.quote: the court finds that the questions of law or fact common to class members predominate over any questions affecting only individual members, and that a class action is superior to other available methods for fairly and efficiently adjudicating the controversy.

rubric.point: A certification order must define the class and claims and appoint class counsel; this one did not appoint counsel.
rubric.quote: An order that certifies a class action must define the class and the class claims, issues, or defenses, and must appoint class counsel under Rule 23(g).

rubric.point: For a (b)(3) class the court must direct the best practicable notice, including individual notice to identifiable members; a newspaper ad alone does not meet that standard.
rubric.quote: the court must direct to class members the best notice that is practicable under the circumstances, including individual notice to all members who can be identified through reasonable effort.

rubric.point: A court of appeals may permit an appeal from a certification order if a petition is filed within 14 days; September 14 is day 13, so the petition is timely, and the grant is discretionary.
rubric.quote: A party must file a petition for permission to appeal with the circuit clerk within 14 days after the order is entered

rubric.point: A certified class's claims may be settled or dismissed only with the court's approval, so the private deal cannot take effect alone.
rubric.quote: The claims, issues, or defenses of a certified class-or a class proposed to be certified for purposes of settlement-may be settled, voluntarily dismissed, or compromised only with the court's approval.

rubric.point: The proposed dismissal would bind the class, so the court must direct notice in a reasonable manner to the bound members if giving notice is justified by the parties' showing that the court will likely be able to approve the proposal under Rule 23(e)(2) and certify the class for purposes of judgment on it; none was directed, and a $5,000 payment to Nolan alone makes that showing doubtful.
rubric.quote: The court must direct notice in a reasonable manner to all class members who would be bound by the proposal if giving notice is justified by the parties' showing that the court will likely be able to:

rubric.point: The court may approve only after a hearing and on finding the proposal fair, reasonable and adequate, considering adequacy of representation and equitable treatment of class members; $5,000 to Nolan alone and nothing for the class makes those findings doubtful.
rubric.quote: the court may approve it only after a hearing and only on finding that it is fair, reasonable, and adequate after considering whether:

rubric.point: The parties must file a statement identifying any agreement made in connection with the proposal, which reaches the $5,000 payment to Nolan.
rubric.quote: The parties seeking approval must file a statement identifying any agreement made in connection with the proposal.

model:
Rule 23(a). All four prerequisites must be met. About 1,800 customers make joinder impracticable (Rule 23(a)(1)). Whether the contract disclosed the fee is common to all (Rule 23(a)(2)). Nolan paid the same fee, so his claim is typical (Rule 23(a)(3)). Nothing shows a conflict at certification, so he adequately represents the class then (Rule 23(a)(4)), though the later deal for him alone cuts the other way.

Rule 23(b)(3). Common questions predominate and a class action is superior: same fee, same disclosure question, small damages.

The order. Rule 23(c)(1)(B) requires an order certifying a class to define the class and claims and appoint class counsel under Rule 23(g). This order appointed none and must be completed. Rule 23(c)(2)(B) requires, for a (b)(3) class, the best notice practicable, including individual notice to members identifiable through reasonable effort. Brightline holds every address, so one newspaper advertisement falls short.

The petition. Rule 23(f) lets a court of appeals permit an appeal from a certification order if a petition is filed with the circuit clerk within 14 days after entry. September 14 is 13 days after September 1, so the petition is timely. Permission is for the court of appeals.

The dismissal. Under Rule 23(e) a certified class's claims may be dismissed only with court approval, so the private deal cannot end the case. Under Rule 23(e)(1)(B) the court must direct notice in a reasonable manner to all class members who would be bound by the proposal, but only if giving notice is justified by the parties' showing that the court will likely be able to approve the proposal under Rule 23(e)(2) and certify the class for purposes of judgment on it. None has been directed, and a $5,000 payment to Nolan alone makes that showing doubtful. Under Rule 23(e)(2) the court may approve only after a hearing and on finding the proposal fair, reasonable and adequate, considering adequacy of representation and equitable treatment of members; $5,000 for Nolan and nothing for the class makes those findings doubtful. Rule 23(e)(3) requires a statement identifying any agreement made in connection with the proposal.
